fields.foundation: The Abbasid Caliphate was founded in 750 CE following the Abbasid Revolution, which overthrew the Umayyad dynasty at the Battle of the Great Zab in January of that year. The revolution grew out of widespread discontent with Umayyad Arab exclusivism, a policy that marginalised non-Arab Muslims, particularly Persian converts known as mawali. Its general was Abu Muslim, a charismatic commander of obscure but probably Persian origin operating from Khorasan. The first caliph, Abu al-Abbas al-Saffah (r. 750–754), inherited the Umayyad territorial empire and faced challenges at once. Shi'a supporters who had expected a dynasty descended from Ali felt betrayed, the Umayyad survivor Abd al-Rahman I escaped to establish a rival emirate in al-Andalus, and Abu Muslim himself remained a dangerous independent power. It was the second caliph, al-Mansur (r. 754–775), who gave the dynasty its lasting form. He had Abu Muslim executed in 755, which removed the most dangerous rival, and in 762 founded the Round City of Baghdad, Madinat al-Salam or "City of Peace". It stood on the western bank of the Tigris not far from the ruins of the Sasanian capital Ctesiphon, a site chosen to connect Abbasid authority to Persian imperial prestige. Baghdad grew within decades into one of the largest cities in the world. Unlike their predecessors, the Abbasids accepted Muslims of every ethnicity, welcomed Persian mawali into the bureaucracy, and presented themselves as the legitimate inheritors of universal Islamic rule.
fields.socioeconomy: The Abbasid Caliphate had one of the most developed economies of the medieval world. Baghdad sat where transcontinental trade routes linking the Mediterranean, Central Asia, the Indian subcontinent and Tang China met, and at its peak it was the commercial hub of the known world. The caliphate drew its revenues from agricultural taxation across Mesopotamia's highly productive Sawad, from customs duties on the Indian Ocean trade passing through the Persian Gulf, and from remittances sent by provincial governors across an empire stretching from North Africa to Central Asia. With Persian administrative traditions came a highly developed system of taxation, record-keeping and land assessment. The Abbasid state was far more cosmopolitan than its predecessor. Persian, Arab and Turkic elements coexisted within the court and administration, and Baghdad's large urban class of merchants, scholars and artisans made the city a centre of culture and learning. The Barmakid family belonged to this mixed elite: they were Persian administrators who served the early caliphs and rose to the height of their power as viziers under Harun al-Rashid until their sudden fall in 803. Agricultural productivity in Mesopotamia remained high through the early period, sustained by the network of canals and irrigation works that had made the region fertile for millennia. The Zanj Rebellion (869–883), a massive revolt of enslaved labourers in southern Iraq, devastated the agricultural heartland and contributed materially to the caliphate's later economic decline.
fields.military: The Abbasid military changed fundamentally over the dynasty's lifetime. In the early period, the caliphate relied on the Khurasani armies that had won the revolution, a mixed Arab and Persian force loyal to the dynasty. Under Harun al-Rashid (r. 786–809), these forces were powerful enough to defeat the Byzantine Emperor Nikephoros I in 806 and impose humiliating tribute terms. The turning point came under al-Mu'tasim (r. 833–842), who built up a professional slave army of Turkic soldiers, the ghilman, recruited from Central Asia. He intended to give the caliph a loyal personal force independent of Arab and Khurasani factions, and moved the capital to Samarra in 836 to house it. The new army fought well in the short term, but it was catastrophic for the caliphate as an institution: the Turkic commanders quickly learned to control the caliphate by murdering any caliph who resisted their demands. The Anarchy at Samarra (861–870) began with the assassination of al-Mutawakkil and saw four caliphs killed by the very army meant to protect them. Military power passed increasingly to provincial commanders and then to outright successor dynasties: the Tahirids, Saffarids and Samanids in the east, and later the Buyids and Seljuks at the centre. The revival under al-Nasir (r. 1180–1225) partially rebuilt caliphal military capacity, enough to secure Baghdad and its hinterland, but the caliphate was never again a first-rank military power.
fields.governance: The Abbasid administrative system was a significant advance on the Umayyad model. Al-Mansur centralised judicial administration and appointed loyal governors across the empire. He also began the vizierate, a chief ministry drawn typically from the Persian bureaucratic tradition, which became the primary instrument of imperial government. The Barmakid family served as viziers and secretaries under several caliphs and built a chancery that managed correspondence, taxation and provincial oversight. The legal system was organised around the developing schools of Islamic jurisprudence (madhhabs). The caliph claimed authority as temporal ruler and also as Commander of the Faithful, the supreme religious and political sovereign. This dual legitimacy was central to Abbasid ideology, and al-Ma'mun (r. 813–833) pushed it furthest by adopting Mu'tazilism as state doctrine and launching the mihna, an inquisition asserting the caliph's right to define theological orthodoxy. The weakness of the system was its dependence on the caliph's personal authority. Once Turkic military commanders began placing and removing caliphs at will after 861, the bureaucracy continued to function but the political coherence it depended on was hollow. Under Buyid domination (945–1055), the caliphs retained religious prestige but exercised little or no political authority. In effect they sanctified the rulers who held actual power.
fields.impact: The Abbasid Caliphate's influence on the world was greater even than its enormous territory would suggest, chiefly because of its part in generating, preserving and transmitting knowledge. The House of Wisdom (Bayt al-Hikma), traditionally associated with Harun al-Rashid and reaching its zenith under al-Ma'mun, sponsored the systematic translation of Greek, Persian, Indian and Syriac texts into Arabic. The project preserved Aristotle, Euclid, Galen and Claudius Ptolemy for the medieval world. Al-Khwarizmi's treatise on calculation by completion and balancing (al-Kitāb al-mukhtaṣar fī ḥisāb al-jabr wal-muqābala, c. 820), the work that gave algebra its name, was written in this environment and permanently changed mathematics. The caliphate's trade and diplomatic networks reached Tang China, the East African coast and the court of Charlemagne, and they made Arabic a language of international commerce and scholarship. The Abbasid model of multi-ethnic Islamic government, with all Muslims under a single religious-political authority, became the template against which later Islamic states measured themselves. Even after the Mongol destruction of Baghdad in 1258, the shadow caliphate maintained by the Mamluks in Cairo (1261–1517) gave legitimacy to Muslim rulers across North Africa and the Levant. The learning of the Abbasid Golden Age was recovered through Arabic translations in Sicily and Spain, and later European science was built in part upon it.
fields.decline: The Abbasid Caliphate declined for a reason that lay in its own founding success. By opening the empire to Muslims of all ethnicities, the Abbasids enabled the rise of Persian, Turkic and other non-Arab power centres that eventually eclipsed the caliphs themselves. The Turkic ghilman army built up by al-Mu'tasim began the military subjugation of the caliphate; the Anarchy at Samarra (861–870) made it irreversible. The Zanj Rebellion (869–883) wrecked the agricultural economy of southern Iraq. The Buyid takeover of Baghdad in 945 removed the last vestiges of caliphal political authority and reduced the institution to a religious symbol, and the Seljuks who replaced the Buyids in 1055 maintained the same arrangement. A partial revival under al-Nasir (r. 1180–1225) raised brief hopes of genuine restoration, but the Mongol invasion ended the Baghdad caliphate entirely. Hulagu Khan's forces took the city in February 1258, executed Caliph al-Musta'sim, and sacked its libraries, including the House of Wisdom. The shadow caliphate continued in Cairo under Mamluk patronage until 1517, when the Ottoman Sultan Selim I's conquest of Egypt brought even that ceremonial institution to an end.
fields.summary: The Abbasid Caliphate lasted in one form or another for 767 years. Its religious legitimacy survived even as its political substance was repeatedly hollowed out. Its fall was the definitive end of a unified caliphal authority, and the caliphal institution remained fragmented from then on. It is remembered as the civilisation that gave the medieval world algebra, advances in astronomy and medicine, and the preservation of classical learning, achievements that outlasted by centuries the political empire that produced them.
fields.teaser: The Abbasid golden age brought major advances in mathematics, astronomy, medicine and philosophy, as scholars translated and built on Greek, Persian and Indian learning. Baghdad, home of the House of Wisdom, was a great centre of scholarship.
fields.t0: The Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads in 750 and ruled a multi-ethnic Islamic empire from their new capital, Baghdad.
fields.t1: Baghdad's House of Wisdom translated Greek, Persian and Indian learning into Arabic and helped give the world algebra.
fields.t2: Turkic slave soldiers, then Buyid and Seljuk overlords, hollowed out caliphal power long before the Mongols sacked Baghdad in 1258.
fields.dyk: The word 'algebra' comes from al-jabr in the title of al-Khwarizmi's treatise on calculation, written in Abbasid Baghdad around 820.
